title: Not Just Stone: 66-Million-Year-Old Dino Bone Yields Original Collagen, Shaking Up Paleontology
summary:
For most of modern paleontology, dinosaur fossils were considered chemically dead — mineralized skeletons with no original biological material left. Time, heat, and pressure were thought to destroy everything organic. But a groundbreaking study on a 66-million-year-old Edmontosaurus sacrum — a 22-kilogram hip bone from South Dakota's Hell Creek Formation — is forcing a major rethink. Researchers led by the University of Liverpool have detected genuine collagen fragments, the primary structural protein in bone, using an arsenal of advanced techniques including protein sequencing and multiple forms of mass spectrometry.

This isn't the first claim of ancient proteins. Since Mary Schweitzer's controversial 2005 report of soft tissue in a T. rex femur, the field has been bitterly divided. Skeptics argued such finds were modern contamination or bacterial residue. What sets this new study apart is its rigorous, multi-pronged approach. The team combined microscopy, chemical analysis, and protein sequencing on the same fossil, even identifying hydroxyproline — an amino acid uniquely abundant in bone collagen — to rule out contamination. "This research shows beyond doubt that organic biomolecules, such as proteins like collagen, appear to be present in some fossils," said Professor Steve Taylor, chair of the Mass Spectrometry Research Group at Liverpool. "It refutes the hypothesis that any organics found in fossils must result from contamination."

The implications are staggering. If proteins can survive for tens of millions of years, scientists gain a revolutionary tool to study extinct animals. Molecular traces could reveal evolutionary relationships invisible to the naked eye, or unlock secrets about dinosaur growth, aging, and disease. Taylor suggests researchers may need to revisit fossil samples collected over the past century — old cross-polarized light microscopy images might contain overlooked evidence of preserved collagen. "This could unlock new insights into dinosaurs, for example revealing connections between dinosaur species that remain unknown," he added.

The discovery, published in Analytical Chemistry, also raises a profound question: how did these fragile molecules survive? Understanding the preservation mechanism could rewrite what we know about fossilization. For now, the Edmontosaurus sacrum stands as a landmark — a molecular time capsule that promises to bring the age of dinosaurs into sharper focus than ever before.
why_it_matters: Understanding how biological materials survive millions of years could redefine our search for ancient life on Earth and other planets, and help explain mass extinctions.

background_read: In 2005, paleontologist Mary Schweitzer (a researcher at North Carolina State University) stunned the world by reporting soft tissue and possible protein remnants inside a 68-million-year-old Tyrannosaurus rex femur. However, many experts argued that these organic traces were simply contamination from modern microbes or lab handling.

The new study, led by the University of Liverpool (a prominent British research institution), tackled this controversy head-on with a multi-technique approach. The fossil chosen was a sacrum (hip bone) from an Edmontosaurus, a common duck-billed dinosaur that lived right before the mass extinction 66 million years ago.

The bone was unearthed in South Dakota's Hell Creek Formation, a famous fossil site that has yielded countless dinosaurs from the late Cretaceous period. The results were published in Analytical Chemistry, a scientific journal where studies are rigorously peer-reviewed, giving the findings strong credibility.

This discovery joins a growing body of evidence that original biomolecules can survive far longer than previously thought. If proteins can persist for tens of millions of years, scientists may be able to answer questions about dinosaur evolution, growth rates, and even diseases that fossilized bones alone cannot.

perspectives.description: Researchers can now use collagen to trace dinosaur family trees, growth rates, and health, opening a new molecular window into the past. This could solve long-standing debates about dinosaur physiology and behavior.

Some scientists may still argue that contamination is possible, and the rarity of such preserved proteins means the findings might not be generalizable to all fossils. Extraordinary claims require repeated verification.

The study highlights a tension in paleontology between traditional bone morphology and emerging molecular techniques. It forces a re-evaluation of many museum specimens that may have been dismissed as merely mineralized.

Future missions searching for ancient life on Mars or icy moons could adapt these techniques to detect biomolecules. This work serves as a blueprint for how we might recognize the signs of extinct extraterrestrial organisms.
